A1.justification: Both PDFs describe HyperMARL and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–J. The added material and renumbering in v4 do not prevent reliable comparison.

before.justification: v3 reports original reinforcement-learning experiments, policy-diversity and gradient measurements, ablations, and computational scaling results.

after.justification: v4 retains those empirical results and adds BPS experiments, learned-embedding measurements, and SMAX hyperparameter sensitivity results.

M1.justification: The linear and MLP hypernetworks, agent conditioning, initialization, gradient decoupling, and Algorithm 1 are retained. A2C is added as an experimental backbone without introducing a new HyperMARL component or changing its general procedure.

E1.justification: v4 adds four Blind-Particle Spread scenarios with 15–30 agents, three or five hidden colour-defined roles, and balanced or uneven group sizes (Appendices G.1 and H.2). This substantially extends coverage to role inference without observing agents' assigned colours and to larger heterogeneous teams. Existing environments are retained.

E2.justification: SePS, explicitly excluded in v3 Table 4, becomes an evaluated comparator in v4 Table 8 alongside NoPS and FuPS+ID. The comparator sets in the retained experiments remain unchanged; the reordered MATD3 columns do not introduce different methods.

E3.justification: New study-specific protocols include A2C training on BPS for 20 million timesteps, an end-of-training cosine-distance embedding comparison, and a SMAX sweep over learning rates, embedding dimensions, and hidden architectures. Previously specified training budgets, evaluation procedures, and hyperparameter tables are retained.

E4.justification: Section 6.2 adds a direct examination of learned embedding geometry under shared versus distinct Navigation goals. Appendix F.5 adds systematic SMAX sensitivity analysis. These provide substantial new evidence about representation adaptation and tuning sensitivity beyond the retained gradient-decoupling, initialization, and scaling analyses.

E5.justification: Section 6.2 introduces per-seed embedding distributions and a one-sample t-test against the initial cosine distance of 1.0, reporting p = 0.0079 for shared goals. Existing repeated-run counts and confidence-interval practices are retained; no increase in runs for the retained experiments is reported.

E6.justification: Tables 5 and 8 and Figure 9 add sensitivity, BPS, and embedding results. For example, BPS-4 reports HyperMARL −389.5 versus SePS −411.6, with overlapping confidence intervals. Retained benchmark values and plots are unchanged, including the reordered MATD3 results. Some new CI-overlap markers are inconsistent with the printed intervals.

T1.justification: The method equations, specialization definition in Appendix C, game definitions and Theorem 1 proof in Appendix E, and gradient covariance derivation in Appendix F.2 are retained. The new empirical diagnostics do not introduce substantive theoretical results.

C1.justification: The advertised evaluation expands from 18 scenarios, up to 20 agents, and five baselines to 22 scenarios, up to 30 agents, and six baselines. The central claims about adaptive behaviour through gradient-decoupled hypernetworks remain. The gradient-conflict finding is foregrounded more strongly but was already present in v3.

C2.justification: v4 interprets embedding alignment under shared goals and preserved separation under distinct goals as task-dependent adaptation. It also suggests that smaller embeddings may facilitate homogeneous behaviour in SMAX. Existing gradient-decoupling explanations and parameter-overhead limitations are retained.

D1.justification: Appendix H.2 documents reuse of the SePS implementation and settings, plus BPS learning-rate and hidden-width sweeps. Table 5 specifies the sensitivity configurations, and the MATD3 table clarifies the shared critic for independent actors. Existing hyperparameter tables, computational-resource disclosures, and code URL remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 7 expands comparisons with parameter-sharing approaches, particularly AdaPS and GradPS, explaining differences involving clustering, pruning, and gradient-conflict thresholds. Five cited works are added. CASH was already discussed in v3; its relationship to HyperMARL is clarified rather than newly introduced.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion are substantially rewritten and reorganized around gradient conflict and the decoupling hypothesis. Section 6 gains separate ablation and embedding-analysis subsections, related work is expanded, and acknowledgements and a conference checklist are added. Cross-references and wording also receive corrections.

P2.justification: v4 adds the embedding plot, sensitivity and BPS tables, and a BPS environment panel. It relabels v3's tabular Figure 3 as Table 1, reorders MATD3 columns, and relocates several displays. Existing plot artwork is retained, making this a limited extension and rearrangement of the presentation.

improvement.justification: The SePS comparison addresses an explicit omission in v3, while the embedding and sensitivity analyses strengthen understanding of adaptation and tuning. These are incremental gains over an already extensive evaluation. Some new overlap markers need correction—for example, Table 5's FuPS result at learning rate 0.0003 overlaps the highest-scoring interval despite lacking an asterisk—but the printed intervals still support the cautious competitiveness conclusions.
